power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Multiple viruses can cause acute respiratory infections (ARI), impacting morbidity, mortality and hospital resources.
The objective of this study was to describe viral circulation among patients with ARI, patients' characteristics and severity outcomes.
A retrospective cohort was assembled using electronic health records from the Hospices Civils de Lyon, France.

Adult patients (≥18 years) hospitalised or presenting to the emergency department from October 2016 to April 2025 with either an ICD-10 diagnostic code for ARI or a laboratory-confirmed viral detection were included.
Administrative variables and laboratory results collected during the stay were extracted.
103,011 hospital visits involving 82,077 patients were included.
The number of eligible stays increased substantially since the COVID-19 pandemic, along with year-round laboratory testing.
Following disruption during the pandemic, winter peaks of ARI incidence, influenza and RSV detections reemerged after 2022.
Influenza, rhinovirus and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates peaked in younger adults (<65 years), whereas RSV and hMPV positivity rates were highest in patients aged ≥80 years.
text.formatted: Influenza, rhinovirus and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates peaked in younger adults (<65 years), whereas RSV and hMPV positivity rates were highest in patients aged ≥80 years.

text.text: Patients.

Acute respiratory infections (ARIs) remain a major cause of morbidity, mortality and healthcare utilisation worldwide, particularly during seasonal epidemics and emerging respiratory virus outbreaks 1 .
text.formatted: Acute respiratory infections (ARIs) remain a major cause of morbidity, mortality and healthcare utilisation worldwide, particularly during seasonal epidemics and emerging respiratory virus outbreaks <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> .

text.text: Hospital-based surveillance plays a central role in monitoring the circulation of respiratory pathogens, evaluating disease severity and informing public health interventions 2, 3 .
text.formatted: Hospital-based surveillance plays a central role in monitoring the circulation of respiratory pathogens, evaluating disease severity and informing public health interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: The COVID-19 pandemic further highlighted the importance of timely surveillance systems capable of tracking changes in respiratory virus epidemiology, healthcare demand and diagnostic practices 4.
text.formatted: The COVID-19 pandemic further highlighted the importance of timely surveillance systems capable of tracking changes in respiratory virus epidemiology, healthcare demand and diagnostic practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref>.

text.text: Electronic health records provide an increasingly important source of real-world data for respiratory surveillance because they capture large numbers of patients managed under routine clinical conditions.

However, existing studies have generally relied either on administrative databases, which identify cases using diagnostic codes, or on prospective surveillance cohorts with systematic virological testing in selected populations or predefined surveillance periods [5] [6] [7] [8] .
text.formatted: However, existing studies have generally relied either on administrative databases, which identify cases using diagnostic codes, or on prospective surveillance cohorts with systematic virological testing in selected populations or predefined surveillance periods <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> .

text.text: While each approach has important strengths, few studies have integrated administrative, clinical and laboratory data within the same healthcare system over an extended period, limiting the ability to jointly describe healthcare utilisation, respiratory virus circulation, patient characteristics and severity outcomes in routine practice 9.
text.formatted: While each approach has important strengths, few studies have integrated administrative, clinical and laboratory data within the same healthcare system over an extended period, limiting the ability to jointly describe healthcare utilisation, respiratory virus circulation, patient characteristics and severity outcomes in routine practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref>.

text.text: The objective of this study was to describe respiratory virus circulation including temporal trends in hospital activity related to ARI, patients' characteristics and severity outcomes in the longitudinal cohort of adult patients with ARI attending the Hospices Civils de Lyon (HCL) from October 2016 to April 2025.

We conducted a retrospective cohort study using routinely collected electronic health record data from HCL, the second largest university hospital in France, serving the city of Lyon and its surrounding metropolitan area (approximately 1.4 million inhabitants) 10 .
text.formatted: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using routinely collected electronic health record data from HCL, the second largest university hospital in France, serving the city of Lyon and its surrounding metropolitan area (approximately 1.4 million inhabitants) <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: Administrative records, severity outcomes and laboratory test results generated during routine patient care were linked at the individual hospitalvisit level and pseudonymised prior to analysis.
Eligible patients were adults (≥18 years) who visited an HCL emergency department (ED) or were hospitalised with an ARI from October 1 st , 2016 to April 30 th , 2025.

Patients were included if they had either (i) a laboratory-confirmed detection of influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), human metapneumovirus (hMPV), rhinovirus/enterovirus (RV/EV), adenovirus (ADV), parainfluenza . virus (PIV), or human coronavirus (hCoV), or (ii) at least a diagnostic code corresponding to ARI according to the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) at discharge either from hospital or from any ward during their stay (Supplementary Table 1).
text.formatted: Patients were included if they had either (i) a laboratory-confirmed detection of influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), human metapneumovirus (hMPV), rhinovirus/enterovirus (RV/EV), adenovirus (ADV), parainfluenza . virus (PIV), or human coronavirus (hCoV), or (ii) at least a diagnostic code corresponding to ARI according to the International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) at discharge either from hospital or from any ward during their stay (Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The study covered nine respiratory virus seasons, with epidemic phases considered from October 1 st to April 30 th and interseason periods from May 1 st to September 30 th of each year.
Data for the final 2024-2025 period were available until April 30 th , 2025.
Virological tests did not always enable to distinguish between rhinovirus and enterovirus.
From November 2018, Panther Fusion® respiratory virus assays specific to rhinovirus was implemented at HCL 11 .
text.formatted: From November 2018, Panther Fusion® respiratory virus assays specific to rhinovirus was implemented at HCL <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: Tests for RV/EV or specific to rhinovirus were used subsequently, based on the clinicians' decision.

Administrative variables comprised age, sex, department of residence, date of admission, discharge status (in-hospital death, home or transfer to another healthcare facility), type of hospital visit (hospitalisation or ED visit not followed by a hospitalisation) and ICD-10 diagnostic codes.
Comorbidities were identified from ICD-10 codes assigned during the ARI hospitalisation (Supplementary Table 1).
text.formatted: Comorbidities were identified from ICD-10 codes assigned during the ARI hospitalisation (Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Severity outcomes included length of hospitalisation in days, in-hospital death, admission to an intensive care unit (ICU), use of oxygen supplementation, non-invasive mechanical ventilation (non-IMV), invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) or extra-corporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO).
Laboratory variables included results of virological tests performed during the stay, for any of the viruses used for patient inclusion.

For each hospital visit, multiple virological test results for the same virus were collapsed into a single result, classified as positive if at least one test was positive and negative if all were negative.
All influenza-positive samples were typed; untyped samples were excluded (n=46, all collected before the 2019-2020 season).
Consecutive hospital readmissions occurring within 30 days were considered related to the same hospital visit.
Comorbidities, ICU admission and use of respiratory support were documented from any of these consecutive readmissions within 30 days.

The discharge outcome (home, transfer in another health care setting or in-hospital death) of the final visit was retained, whereas the duration of the first admission was used when analysing length of hospitalisation.
The number of ED visits and hospitalisations included through laboratory-confirmed viral detection or ICD-10 coding were summarised by respiratory virus season.
Visits meeting both inclusion criteria were classified according to laboratory confirmation, which occurred before the diagnostic coding.
Monthly incidence rates of ARI-related hospital visits per 100,000 population were calculated by age group and type of hospital visit using previously estimated HCL catchment populations 12 .
text.formatted: Monthly incidence rates of ARI-related hospital visits per 100,000 population were calculated by age group and type of hospital visit using previously estimated HCL catchment populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: Catchment populations were derived using a proportional patient-flow approach based on population data from Institut National de la Statistique et des Etudes Economiques (INSEE), hospitalisation data from Agence Technique de l'Information sur l'Hospitalisation (ATIH), and, since 2019, ED attendance data from the Réseau d'Urgences d'Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes (Urg'ARA), stratified by age, calendar year and postcode of residence.
Since Urg'ARA started the data collection in 2019, the numbers of patients from the HCL catchment area visiting the ED in 2019 were used for the preceding seasons.
Monthly 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were also reported 13.
text.formatted: Monthly 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were also reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref>.

text.text: Temporal patterns of respiratory virus circulation were described for each virus by season and month using the number of documented laboratory-confirmed detections.
Positivity rates in patients with ARI . were calculated by age group and season for each virus.
The distribution of tested respiratory virus across age groups was also described for each season.

Patient characteristics were summarised separately for hospitalisations and ED-only visits according to sex, age, residence in the Rhône department (the same department as the HCL), readmissions within 30 days and period relative to the COVID-19 pandemic (pre-pandemic: 2016-2017 to 2018-2019; pandemic: 2019-2020 to 2021-2022; post-pandemic: 2022-2023 to 2024-2025).
For hospitalised patients, ED attendance during the stay, number of comorbidities (none, one, or at least two), and individual comorbidities were also described.
Cardiovascular diseases were reported both including and excluding hypertension because of its high prevalence in older adults [14] [15] [16] .
text.formatted: Cardiovascular diseases were reported both including and excluding hypertension because of its high prevalence in older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> .

text.text: Characteristics, laboratory-confirmed viral detection and severity outcomes were additionally summarized by age group (18-64, 65-79 and ≥80 years).

For patients hospitalised after October 1 st , 2020, length of stay and oxygen supplementation were compared between those with laboratory-confirmed influenza A, influenza B, SARS-CoV-2, RSV, hMPV or rhinovirus detection.
Patients with laboratory-confirmed viral co-detections were excluded.
Analyses were stratified by age group (18-64 and ≥65 years) and by ICU admission status, and ventilation interventions were compared only for stays including an admission to ICU.
Statistical testing involving influenza B in patients aged ≥65 years were not performed because of the small number of cases.
Chi-square tests were used to compare categorical variables and either Wilcoxon (for 2-category outcomes) or Kruskal-Wallis (for 3-category outcomes) tests were used for continuous variables.
Pvalues were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, with adjusted p-values <0.05 considered statistically significant 17 .
text.formatted: Pvalues were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, with adjusted p-values <0.05 considered statistically significant <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> .

text.text: Description of severity outcomes for the three age groups are provided in the supplementary material.
All statistical analyses were conducted using R version 4.4.3 18.
text.formatted: All statistical analyses were conducted using R version 4.4.3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref>.

text.text: Overall, 103,011 hospital visits involving 82,077 distinct patients with ARI were identified from October 2016 to April 2025, including 19,948 ED visits without hospitalisation and 83,063 hospitalisations (Figure 1 and Supplementary Table 2).
text.formatted: Overall, 103,011 hospital visits involving 82,077 distinct patients with ARI were identified from October 2016 to April 2025, including 19,948 ED visits without hospitalisation and 83,063 hospitalisations (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> and Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Across the study period, most patients were identified through ICD-10 diagnostic codes rather than laboratory-confirmed viral detection, with 59% of ED visits and 64% of hospitalisations lacking in-hospital virological confirmation.
The number of ARI-related hospital visits increased markedly during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Compared with the 2018-2019 season, hospitalisations increased by 57% in 2020-2021 and remained 53% higher in 2021-2022, while ED visits increased 1.5-fold in 2019-2020, twofold in 2020-2021 and almost threefold in 2021-2022.
After October 2022, the number of ARI hospital visits remained above pre-COVID-19 pandemic levels, with approximately 30% more hospitalisations and twice as many ED visits than before the pandemic.
The proportion of ARI visits with a laboratory-confirmed viral detection increased over time.
Among ED visits, laboratory-confirmed cases increased from 8.7% in 2018-2019 to 62% in 2021-2022, while for hospitalisations they increased from 15% to 58% over the same period.
After October 2021, ED visits surpassed hospitalisations in terms of the proportion of visits with laboratory confirmation.
Monthly incidence rates in the HCL catchment population showed marked seasonal peaks before the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly for hospitalisations in older adults (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Monthly incidence rates in the HCL catchment population showed marked seasonal peaks before the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly for hospitalisations in older adults (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: During the pandemic, incidence patterns changed substantially across all age groups.
Hospitalisation incidences in adults aged 18-64 years and 65-79 years increased from 2020-2021 before declining after October 2022, although remaining above pre-pandemic levels.
Historical seasonal patterns were observed again after the COVID-19 pandemic.
In contrast, ED visits incidence in adults aged ≥65 years increased progressively throughout the pandemic and remained persistently high thereafter.
The COVID-19 pandemic was associated with major changes in respiratory virus testing and detection (Figure 3; Supplementary Figures 1 and 3).
text.formatted: The COVID-19 pandemic was associated with major changes in respiratory virus testing and detection (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>; Supplementary Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: During the 2020-2021 season, influenza and most other respiratory viruses were rarely detected, whereas SARS-CoV-2 accounted for the majority of laboratory-confirmed detections.

From 2022 onwards, both the number of respiratory virus tests and the number of laboratory-confirmed detections increased substantially for all viruses except influenza B, which continued to display high circulation every other year.
Testing outside the traditional respiratory virus season became common after the COVID-19 pandemic for all viruses (Supplementary Figure 1).
text.formatted: Testing outside the traditional respiratory virus season became common after the COVID-19 pandemic for all viruses (Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Despite this expansion in testing, influenza and RSV continued to exhibit well-defined winter epidemic seasonality with very few detections between May and September (Figure 3B). hMPV cases were generally detected from November to May, whereas SARS-CoV-2 and rhinovirus displayed less distinct seasonal patterns.

text.text: Positivity rates differed by age group (Supplementary Figure 2).

text.text: Since the 2019-2020 season, influenza, rhinovirus and SARS-CoV-2 positivity rates were generally highest in adults aged 18-64 years, whereas RSV and hMPV positivity rates were highest in adults aged ≥80 years, except during the 2020-2021 season when low circulation of these viruses.
Most hospital visits involved patients residing in the Rhône department, at a stable rate over time (Table 1).

text.text: Influenza detection was generally associated with shorter hospitalisation (for Influenza A, median duration of 4 days for patients aged 18-64 years and 8 days for those aged ≥65 years without ICU) than SARS-CoV-2 (median 5 and 10 days), RSV and rhinovirus (median 6 and 10 days) and hMPV (median 7 and 10.5).
In younger adults, detection of hMPV, followed by rhinovirus, and RSV in absence of ICU admission, were generally associated with longer stays.
For patients admitted to ICU after October 2020, the use of respiratory support depended on the nature of the detected virus (Figure 5).

text.text: Oxygen supplementation and non-IMV were more frequent in inpatients with RSV or hMPV detections in both age groups.

In young adults, rhinovirus detection was consistently associated with lower use of oxygen supplementation (33% of stays) and ventilatory support (27% for non-IMV and 18% for IMV) than influenza A, SARS-CoV-2, RSV or hMPV detection (52-65% for oxygen support, 42-60% for non-IMV and 34-56% for IMV).

In adults aged ≥65 years, RSV detection was associated with higher use of oxygen supplementation (81%) and non-IMV (74%) than detection of influenza A, SARS-CoV-2 and rhinovirus (52-60% for oxygen supplementation, 35-58% for non-IMV), whereas IMV was most frequently required in patients with either RSV, hMPV or SARS-CoV-2 detection (37-40%).
This study describes a large longitudinal cohort of adults presenting with ARI to a major tertiary university hospital over nine consecutive respiratory virus seasons.

While large real-world studies have successfully used administrative healthcare data to investigate respiratory infections, they have generally relied on diagnostic coding to identify pathogen-specific hospitalisation 6, 7 .
text.formatted: While large real-world studies have successfully used administrative healthcare data to investigate respiratory infections, they have generally relied on diagnostic coding to identify pathogen-specific hospitalisation <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: Conversely, prospective studies incorporating systematic virological testing have usually been limited to specific viruses, selected populations or predefined surveillance periods, often restricted to the winter [19] [20] [21] [22] 8 .
text.formatted: Conversely, prospective studies incorporating systematic virological testing have usually been limited to specific viruses, selected populations or predefined surveillance periods, often restricted to the winter <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: By linking routinely collected administrative data with laboratory-confirmed detections, the cohort in this study captures the main respiratory viruses within the second largest hospital in France.
The COVID-19 pandemic fundamentally changed both respiratory virus epidemiology and hospital diagnostic practices.

In addition to the emergence of SARS-CoV-2, the widespread implementation of molecular diagnostics and the expansion of respiratory virus testing beyond the traditional winter season has led to a large increase in the number of laboratory-confirmed respiratory detections 23 .
text.formatted: In addition to the emergence of SARS-CoV-2, the widespread implementation of molecular diagnostics and the expansion of respiratory virus testing beyond the traditional winter season has led to a large increase in the number of laboratory-confirmed respiratory detections <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> .

text.text: Consequently, temporal increases in virus detections after 2020 should not be interpreted only as evidence of changing virus circulation.

These findings illustrate an important consideration when interpreting routinely collected hospital data: observed temporal changes may result from evolving testing strategies as well as real epidemiological trends.

Similar observations have been reported for RSV, where linkage of microbiological and administrative data substantially improved case ascertainment 24 , while adjustment for under-ascertainment has been estimated to more than double RSV hospitalisation rates in older adults 25.
text.formatted: Similar observations have been reported for RSV, where linkage of microbiological and administrative data substantially improved case ascertainment <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> , while adjustment for under-ascertainment has been estimated to more than double RSV hospitalisation rates in older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">25</ref>.

text.text: Despite these changes in testing practices, the epidemiological patterns observed in our study were consistent with the established behaviour of respiratory viruses in temperate climates.

Influenza and RSV maintained pronounced winter seasonality, whereas SARS-CoV-2 and rhinovirus showed less clearly defined seasonal patterns 26, 27 . hMPV circulated predominantly between late autumn and spring, and together with RSV showed the highest positivity rates in adults ≥80 years, consistent with previous reports describing the burden of these viruses in older adults 20, [28] [29] [30] .

text.text: Influenza and rhinovirus positivity rates, in contrast, were generally highest in younger adults.

Excluding the pre-pandemic period, SARS-CoV-2 was the most frequently detected virus, followed by influenza and RSV, similar to observations from a study in a German tertiary hospital, in which only SARS-CoV-2 screening was systematic 31 .

text.text: By the 2024-2025 season, influenza had again become the predominant respiratory virus, consistent with surveillance findings from other countries 32 .
text.formatted: By the 2024-2025 season, influenza had again become the predominant respiratory virus, consistent with surveillance findings from other countries <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">32</ref> .

text.text: Nevertheless, direct comparison of positivity rates between studies remains challenging because inclusion criteria, patient populations and testing strategies differ substantially.
Hospitalised patients were predominantly older men with multiple comorbidities, particularly cardiovascular disease, chronic lung disease and diabetes as described in previous studies 8, 19, 21, 33 .
text.formatted: Hospitalised patients were predominantly older men with multiple comorbidities, particularly cardiovascular disease, chronic lung disease and diabetes as described in previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">33</ref> .

text.text: Older patients generally had longer hospitalisations and higher in-hospital mortality rate, whereas ICU admission and respiratory support were more frequent in younger adults, probably reflecting differences in clinical management of frail elderly patients.

Among laboratory-confirmed detections, influenza was generally associated with shorter hospitalisations, while RSV and hMPV more frequently required respiratory support. hMPV involved longer hospitalisations in younger adults.
All these results are in agreement with recent studies in hospitalised adults 29, 30, 34 .
text.formatted: All these results are in agreement with recent studies in hospitalised adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">34</ref> .

text.text: The relatively longer hospital stays observed in some patients with rhinovirus detection who did not require ICU admission may reflect the selective testing of patients with greater clinical complexity or underlying chronic disease rather than purely greater intrinsic pathogenicity of rhinovirus, consistent with prospective studies showing that rhinovirus frequently affects older adults with multiple comorbidities 8, 35.

text.text: A major strength of this study was the integration of routinely collected administrative variables, severity outcomes and laboratory data for more than 100,000 ARI-related hospital visits over almost a decade.

Unlike administrative databases alone, the linkage of patients' characteristics and microbiological data improved pathogen ascertainment, while the availability of age-and time-specific catchment populations enabled calculation of population-based incidence rates.

Such real-world datasets are becoming increasingly valuable for respiratory surveillance, disease burden estimation and evaluation of preventive interventions, particularly when combined with robust population denominators 12 .
text.formatted: Such real-world datasets are becoming increasingly valuable for respiratory surveillance, disease burden estimation and evaluation of preventive interventions, particularly when combined with robust population denominators <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> .

text.text: These data could also be used to identify early predictors of patient deterioration, in order to improve their care and the management of hospital beds during epidemics.
This study has several limitations.
The data were collected as part of routine patient care rather than according to a research protocol and therefore depend on the completeness and accuracy of electronic health records.

Comorbidities were identified from ICD-10 codes assigned during the ARI hospitalisation and may have been incompletely captured, while coding practices may also have evolved over time, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Virological testing strategies changed considerably throughout the study period.
Testing was mostly clinician-directed, with periods of systematic testing of SARS-CoV-2 even for asymptomatic patients.

The possible use of triplex or panel tests to detect several viruses at once also increased the number of negative tests, as, for example, SARS-CoV-2 and RSV may also have been tested for a suspicion of influenza.

This may result in under-. ascertainment of some respiratory viruses and overestimation of others, limiting direct comparison of positivity rates across seasons and comparison with systematically tested cohorts.
Consequently, the observed temporal trends reflect both virus circulation and changes in testing practices.
Viral detection did not necessarily reflect active infection, as prolonged viral shedding can be detected, including in asymptomatic patients.
In addition, comparisons between viruses were descriptive and were not adjusted for differences in patient characteristics or clinical management such as bed occupancies.
The differences should therefore not be interpreted as causal.
Finally, although HCL is the second largest university hospital in France, these findings originate from a single healthcare network and may not be fully generalisable to other healthcare settings.
In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive description of nearly a decade of real-world data on adults with ARI in a large tertiary healthcare hospital.

Beyond documenting changes in respiratory virus epidemiology before, during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, it illustrates how evolving diagnostic practices influence the interpretation of routinely collected surveillance data.

By integrating administrative data, severity outcomes and laboratory information with population-based denominators, this cohort provides a platform for respiratory surveillance and further analyses of disease burden, severity and healthcare use.
In particular, future analyses of these data could help identify predictive risk factors of severity, detect at-risk patients early and tailor adequate care.
